Zhongliang was like a man transformed. He grew sociable, fell in with the ways of the others, took to talking of women with the rest of the postmen, and liked to go drinking with them after work, off to anywhere at all that spared him going home. Zhou San marked it all, but in the depths of Zhongliang's eyes he saw as well a man's black brooding. This day, as the men crowded and jostled at the sorting-room window, Zhou San leaned in, clapped Zhongliang on the shoulder for all to see, and said this fellow grew more like his old man by the day, down to the very turn of his speech. Zhongliang ignored him. He loathed now every word Zhou San spoke, but he never once crossed his look. "When you pass the Taishun tea shop," Zhou San said, without a flicker, "remember to step in and ask. If they've any tea dust, bring me back half a catty."
What it meant was that intelligence was to go out by way of the tea shop, and they were to make ready in advance.

It was coming out of the tea shop that Zhongliang noticed he was being followed. He got on his bicycle, ducked into one lane, and, coming out of another, saw Su Lina standing by a telephone pole at the lane mouth. She wore a cheongsam of Indian silk, a cream trench coat over it. This was the second time she had spoken to Zhongliang. She said, "I want to see Mr. Pan."
Zhongliang looked at her. At a moment like this any sign at all was against the rules. Zhongliang could only look at her.
"Tell your handler: say that the cuckoo is singing." With that Su Lina lifted her face and walked off. The click of her high heels on the cement was plain to hear.

At dusk, when Zhongliang passed the two sentences on to Zhou San, Zhou San spread open the packet of tea dust and grumbled on and on that a year ago this price would have bought two ounces of Biluochun.
Two days later Zhou San handed Zhongliang a wad of money and an address.

In a cramped little room Zhongliang saw Su Lina again, the fine clothes on her at odds with the bare furnishings. Zhongliang set the money on the table and said, standing, "When a meeting is needed, Mr. Pan will contact you."
"I need to meet now." Su Lina too was standing. "I've waited in this godforsaken place a year, two months, and nine days."
Zhongliang was startled and said, "Go and find yourself work."
"Find it where?" Su Lina pointed out the window at the street, where crowds stood in line for relief. "If there were work, would they queue here every day for two loaves of bread?"
"These are your superiors' instructions," said Zhongliang. "Just those two sentences."
Su Lina was startled, propped herself on the table, and sat slowly down. "Go," she said.
Zhongliang went to the door, thought better of it, turned back, and said suddenly, "The letters from the war zone are all held in the Japanese Tokko."

Su Lina's head came up at once. Mr. Pan had said the same thing, at their last meeting. Mr. Pan had brought her word that the 88th Division had been broken at the Battle of Changsha, a force of twenty thousand cut to under eight hundred. "You should have stopped him going to the front," Mr. Pan had said. "He was worth more to us kept in the rear."

"Can you stop a man from serving his country?" Su Lina had said, her eyes fixed unmoving on the screen, and after a long moment, as if to herself, "If he were dead, I should have had the notice of it."
"Every letter from the war zone is held in the Tokko." Mr. Pan had said, "You have to leave the Siming Apartments."
"Is there any need?" Su Lina had said. "The concession is full of officers' families, and all their men are fighting the Japanese."

"Are you the same as they are?" By long practice the Japanese would watch and investigate everyone tied to the resistance, their families included. Mr. Pan had said, "I don't want anything happening that touches the organization."
"And if he comes back and can't find me?"
"Your task is finished."
"But I've married him. I'm his wife."
"First of all you are a soldier." Mr. Pan had said, "Your task now is to go to ground where you are."
Su Lina had sat on dully in her seat, and only when the film ended did she find that Mr. Pan had long since gone, without her ever noticing the tracks of tears dried on her cheeks.

The scene in the Paramount ballroom was grander than ever, the hostesses' charity benefit dance in full swing. When Zhongliang appeared among the crowd in a Western suit, his hair combed to a shine, Su Lina could hardly believe her eyes. By now she was the reigning hostess of the place.

When the two of them were halfway through a mournful jazz number, Su Lina said, "You shouldn't be a postman." Zhongliang said nothing, only held her waist with great care. Su Lina said again, "And still less should you be here."
"I've come on Mr. Pan's behalf," said Zhongliang. "He sends his regards."

Su Lina's eyes went all at once sharp and clear, and after a moment a bitter smile showed on her face. "So you've done well for yourself these few years," she said. Zhongliang said, "Mr. Pan hopes you'll be chosen queen of this year's dance."
Su Lina gave a cold laugh and said, "He doesn't need me to go to ground anymore?"
"He wants you to get close to a man, and win his trust." Zhongliang said, "Mr. Pan says you'll understand. And he says: whatever sacrifice we make is worth the making."
Su Lina said not a word. Suddenly she laid her head on Zhongliang's shoulder and moved with his steps, like a boat that drifts where the current takes it.
Zhongliang held his breath and said, "If you won't take this task, I'll explain it upward for you."
Su Lina still said nothing, and only when the number ended did she say, amid the applause, "Who is he?"
"I'll give you the file tomorrow," said Zhongliang.
Su Lina nodded, took his arm, and walked with him to the donation box, where all at once she gave a lovely smile and said, "Give something for the war of resistance, sir."
Zhongliang gently brushed her hand aside and pushed out through the crowd without looking back.

The next day Zhongliang put a man's photograph into her hand. Su Lina thought at once of the evening before Zhou Chukang left Shanghai, the man in the white linen shirt with the folding fan, the one who had said, "Mrs. Zhou."

Qin Zhaokuan: graduated 1929 from the politics department of Tokyo Imperial University, returned to China in 1931; when Wang Jingwei became Foreign Minister in 1935, he was taken on as Wang's Japanese interpreter, and had just now been named liaison officer for Shanghai affairs of the Wang puppet government. His open identity in the concession was general manager of the Dahua Trading Company, in charge of intelligence exchange with the Japanese side, and he was a welcome guest at No. 76 Jessfield Road. Zhongliang reeled it off like a lesson, looked at Su Lina, and added, "From today, I'm your courier. I'll handle all your contact with the higher-ups."
Su Lina said nothing, but struck a match and set the photograph alight.
Zhongliang hesitated, then said, "Then we begin."
Su Lina gave a nod, stood, and said lightly, "I've an appointment with the tailor. I'm going for a fitting."

On the night Su Lina was chosen queen of the dance, the Paramount was thick with the city's notables. The general manager of the Dahua Trading Company came as an invited guest. After crowning Su Lina, Qin Zhaokuan smiled and said, "Mrs. Zhou. I never thought to see you here."
Su Lina looked awkward, at a loss, and only bowed her head to breathe in the bunch of flowers in her hands.

All that evening the look on Su Lina's face was at odds with the merriment around her, and while she partnered Qin Zhaokuan through a number, she could not help asking whether he had any news of Chukang. Qin Zhaokuan shook his head. Su Lina said, "You know so many people. Couldn't you help me ask?"
Qin Zhaokuan thought, sighed, and said, "To find one man in times like these is no better than fishing a needle out of the sea."

Su Lina said no more. She went back to the table and drank, cup after cup after cup. Qin Zhaokuan sat across from her, drawing on a cigar, watching her with an easy, elegant calm, and only when the music ended and the guests had gone did he take her arm, leave by the Paramount's back door, and drive her home.
Qin Zhaokuan stood before her pitch-dark room, sighed, and said, "You shouldn't be living in a place like this."
Su Lina paid him no mind, went reeling inside, shut the door hard, and, without so much as switching on the light, threw herself down on the bed and, after a long while, began to wail aloud.

Some months later, on the day she moved into the flat Qin Zhaokuan had prepared for her, Su Lina left a coverless copy of The Young Companion on the windowsill. It was the signal that the plan was going smoothly. When Zhongliang passed below the window at dusk and saw the pictorial, it was as though a fist struck him full in the chest, and his face went white in an instant.

That day Qin Zhaokuan took Su Lina to a dinner at the home of the Japanese intelligence officer Nakamura Nobuo. In the car Su Lina looked at him and said, "You're a businessman. What are you doing mixed up with the Japanese?"
Qin Zhaokuan smiled and said, "Do you dislike the Japanese so much as that?"
"Not dislike. Hate." Su Lina looked out at the streets sliding past. "If not for them, I'd never have fallen to what I am today."

The smile left Qin Zhaokuan's face; he held the wheel with both hands and said not another word, until they had passed into the entrance hall of Nakamura Nobuo's residence, where he took Su Lina's hand and, to the Japanese intelligence officer who came to meet them, introduced her: "This is my fiancée."
Nakamura Nobuo, in a loose, wide kimono, looked like an old Japanese farmer. He bowed to the faintly bewildered Su Lina, then smiled and said a string of Japanese to Qin Zhaokuan.
In the car back, Qin Zhaokuan said, smiling, "Nakamura says you're the most beautiful woman he's ever seen. He says too that he envies us Chinese men."
Su Lina said coldly, "I'm not your fiancée."
"After tonight you are." Qin Zhaokuan said, "I mean to marry you."
Su Lina lowered her head and said softly, "And I won't be your concubine."
"Why?" Qin Zhaokuan pondered, then said, "Is there still any meaning in waiting for him?"
Su Lina shook her head and said, "I'm waiting for no one."
Qin Zhaokuan sighed, put an arm around her, and drew her head down onto his shoulder. As the car came round a bend, he said suddenly, "I'll wait."
